title: The Glow in the Shed: The Curies and the Race for the Rays
subtitle: X-rays, uranium rays, polonium, radium and transmutation — Würzburg, Paris, Montreal, Stockholm
intro: In eleven years, from a darkened room in Würzburg in November 1895 to a rain-slick street on the Left Bank in April 1906, physics found out that atoms are not permanent. The story is usually told as one woman's triumph, and Marie Curie earns that. But the record is a relay and a race. A German professor saw a screen glow across his laboratory. A Paris physicist, nudged by a question at the Académie, wrapped photographic plates in black paper and was rescued by bad weather. A Polish doctoral student chose his rays for her thesis because no one had yet written much about them, and within months she was racing a German she had never met.

This chapter is built less from diaries than from the instruments of priority: laboratory notebooks, papers whose dates were fixed by the weekly sittings of the Académie des sciences, manuscripts signed off with a place and a day, and letters that bent a prize. That is said plainly here because it is the honest shape of the record. Röntgen had most of his personal papers burned on his own instruction. Becquerel speaks to us through short notes in the Comptes rendus. The Curies' own laboratory notebooks survive at the Bibliothèque nationale de France, so contaminated by the radium they handled that readers sign a waiver and the most affected sheets are encapsulated.

Lay the dates side by side and the race becomes visible. Gerhard Schmidt told the German Physical Society on 24 March 1898 that thorium gives off Becquerel rays; Marie Curie's note saying the same, and more, was presented in Paris nineteen days later. In Cambridge, Ernest Rutherford dated his manuscript naming alpha and beta rays on 1 September 1898; in Paris the Curies were already writing 'radio-active' into the title of their polonium note. In Montreal on 13 September 1899 Rutherford signed off a paper describing a radiation that fell to half its strength in about a minute — the first clear measurement of what would be called a half-life — while across the Atlantic André Debierne was drawing yet another new substance out of the Curies' pitchblende residues.

Then the human seam. When the French Academy's eminent members put forward Becquerel and Pierre Curie for the 1903 Nobel Prize, Marie's name was not on their letters. A Swedish mathematician, Gösta Mittag-Leffler, warned Pierre; Pierre wrote back that he wished to be considered together with her. The archive shows another nomination, by Charles Bouchard, that named all three. The book reports these documents as positions in the record, not as a verdict.

The chapter ends with the accident of 19 April 1906 and the private journal Marie kept for a year afterwards, addressed to Pierre. That journal is a twentieth-century publication and is digested here, never quoted. Two codas reach forward: her second Nobel Prize in 1911, and the autumn of 1914, when she and seventeen-year-old Irène drove X-ray cars — Röntgen's rays, nineteen years on — to the wounded at the front.
calendar_note: All dates are Gregorian (France, Germany, Britain, Canada and Sweden all used it). Dates given for Comptes rendus notes are the dates of the Académie's Monday sittings at which a note was presented; printed issues followed within days. Manuscript dates (e.g. Rutherford's 'Cavendish Laboratory, September 1, 1898') are the signing-off dates printed at the foot of the papers, earlier than the journal issue dates.

eyes.name: Marie Skłodowska Curie
eyes.role: Polish-born doctoral student (aged 30 in 1897), then teacher at Sèvres and physicist; first woman to receive a doctorate in France (1903)
eyes.side: Paris; ESPCI laboratory with Pierre Curie
eyes.where: The ESPCI workshop and storeroom, rue Vauquelin, Paris

waypoints.label: Sorbonne: doctoral defence, 25 June 1903; Pierre's chair, 1906

eyes.authenticity: Laboratory notebooks (1897–1898 onward) kept jointly with Pierre are held at the BnF (fonds entered 1970 after decontamination and microfilming); still contaminated by radium. Her Comptes rendus notes are dated publications. Her 1906–07 mourning journal is held at the BnF; extracts appeared in Ève Curie's 1937 biography and it has since been printed in French (an Odile Jacob edition of 2022 presents it with her 'Pierre Curie'; publishers' descriptions of its earlier publication history differ). No quotations are used from any of these. Ève Curie's 'Madame Curie' (1937) is a later family biography — used only as flagged context.
eyes.bio: She chose Becquerel's uranium rays as a thesis subject because they were new and little explored, measured them with an electrometer built on Pierre's piezoelectric quartz, and turned a measurement into a hunt for new elements. Her angle is that of the person whose numbers drove everything and whose credit was repeatedly at risk of being folded into her husband's.

sources.title: BnF — Un héritage qui rayonne: les carnets de Marie Curie
Giunta (trans.), M. Curie, 'Rays emitted by compounds of uranium and of thorium' (1898), annotated
AIP exhibit: Marie Curie and the Science of Radioactivity

eyes.name: Pierre Curie
eyes.role: Physicist, professor at ESPCI (aged 38 in 1897), co-discoverer of piezoelectricity; from 1904 professor at the Sorbonne
eyes.where: ESPCI, rue Vauquelin; killed in rue Dauphine, 19 April 1906
eyes.vantage_label: principal: co-author and second hand in the notebooks
eyes.authenticity: Shares the BnF notebooks with Marie; his letters to Mittag-Leffler (6 August 1903) and to the Swedish Academy (19 November 1903) are documented by the Association Curie et Joliot-Curie. His 1905 Nobel lecture is published by the Nobel Foundation (French original).
eyes.bio: He set aside his own work on crystals and magnetism in 1898 to join Marie's hunt, and his instruments made her measurements possible. His letters of 1903 are the clearest document in this chapter of one scientist insisting on another's credit.

sources.title: Association Curie et Joliot-Curie — The 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics
AIP exhibit — Tragedy and Adjustment (1906–1910)

eyes.name: Antoine Henri Becquerel
eyes.role: Physicist, professor at the Muséum d'histoire naturelle and the École polytechnique (aged 43 in 1896); third generation of a dynasty of phosphorescence specialists
eyes.where: Muséum national d'histoire naturelle, Jardin des Plantes, Paris
eyes.vantage_label: same city: the predecessor whose rays started the hunt
eyes.authenticity: Known through his series of short notes in the Comptes rendus, 1896; his own account in the 2 March note gives the cloudy-day sequence. Annotated English translation by Carmen Giunta.
eyes.bio: He was looking for a link between phosphorescence and Röntgen's rays and found something else. His notes show a careful man revising his hypothesis week by week; he presented the Curies' polonium note to the Académie and shared the 1903 prize with them.

sources.title: Giunta (trans.), Becquerel 1896 notes, annotated
APS News — March 1, 1896: Henri Becquerel discovers radioactivity

eyes.name: Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen
eyes.role: Professor of physics and rector of the University of Würzburg (aged 50 in 1895)
eyes.where: Institute of Physics, Pleicherring (now Röntgenring), Würzburg
eyes.vantage_label: abroad: the German eye that opened the decade
eyes.authenticity: Most personal papers were burned at his direction; the 1888–1900 outgoing mail book survives in the University of Würzburg archives. His 'Über eine neue Art von Strahlen' (submitted 28 December 1895) is the primary record. No diary exists.
eyes.bio: Working alone for weeks, he found that a discharge tube wrapped in black card made a distant screen glow, and that the rays passed through flesh but not bone or metal. His discovery set Poincaré's question, which set Becquerel's experiment, which set Marie Curie's thesis.

sources.title: University of Würzburg — Röntgen exhibition catalogue (English)

eyes.name: Gustave Bémont
eyes.role: Chef de travaux (head of practical chemistry) at ESPCI
eyes.vantage_label: in the lab: the chemist at the bench
eyes.form: co-signed paper; work recorded in the Curie notebooks
eyes.authenticity: His role is documented by his co-signature on the 26 December 1898 radium note and by the ESPCI history; he appears in a c.1898 ESPCI laboratory photograph. No personal diary is known.
eyes.bio: Neither Curie was a trained chemist; Bémont helped them separate pitchblende and concentrate radium-bearing barium chloride. He is the assistant-shaped figure history usually drops, and his name sits beside theirs on the radium paper.

sources.title: ESPCI — History: ESPCI and the discovery of chemical elements
J.-P. Adloff, 'A short history of polonium and radium', Chemistry International 2011

eyes.name: Gerhard Carl Nathaniel Schmidt
eyes.role: German physicist and physical chemist, then at Erlangen
eyes.vantage_label: abroad: the rival who got to thorium first
eyes.authenticity: Talk to the Deutsche Physikalische Gesellschaft on 24 March 1898; paper in Annalen der Physik und Chemie 65 (1898), 141–151, dated 23 April 1898 in the GDCh history. His location at Erlangen in 1898 is from standard biographies (approx).
eyes.bio: He found independently that thorium compounds emit Becquerel rays and said so nineteen days before Marie Curie's note. He did not follow the trail into pitchblende, which is where the new elements were.

sources.title: GDCh Mitteilungen 25 (2017) — history of Schmidt's thorium work
Encyclopedia.com — Schmidt, Gerhard Carl Nathaniel

eyes.name: Ernest Rutherford
eyes.role: New Zealand research student at the Cavendish under J. J. Thomson (aged 27 in 1898); from autumn 1898 Macdonald Professor of Physics at McGill, Montreal
eyes.side: Britain / Canada; Cavendish Laboratory and McGill
eyes.where: Cambridge, then Montreal; in Paris on 25 June 1903
eyes.vantage_label: abroad: the rival school that explained what the rays were
eyes.authenticity: Philosophical Magazine papers, each signed off with place and date; English originals published before 1929, so short quotations are allowed. His account of the 25 June 1903 evening in Paris survives through later biographies (A. S. Eve, 1939) and Ève Curie (1937) — flagged as later.
eyes.bio: He split the uranium radiation into alpha and beta, measured the first half-period, and with Soddy argued that radioactive atoms turn into other atoms. His papers are the English-language mirror of the Paris notebooks.

sources.title: Rutherford 1899, 'Uranium radiation and the electrical conduction produced by it' (text)
Rutherford 1900, 'A radioactive substance emitted from thorium compounds' (text)
Rutherford & Soddy 1902, 'The cause and nature of radioactivity' (excerpt)

eyes.name: Frederick Soddy
eyes.role: English chemist, demonstrator at McGill from 1900 (aged 23), later with Ramsay in London (1903) and at Glasgow (1904)
eyes.vantage_label: abroad: the chemist who said the word 'transmutation'
eyes.authenticity: Joint Philosophical Magazine papers with Rutherford (1902–03). His famous exclamation that their result was transmutation is his own recollection told decades later (via M. Howorth's 1958 biography) and is not quoted here.
eyes.bio: He supplied the chemistry that let Rutherford show thorium was changing into something chemically different. His vantage is the junior partner whose chemical separations made the physical argument undeniable.

sources.title: Chemistry World — Transmutations and isotopes
Rutherford & Soddy 1902 (Giunta)

eyes.name: Gösta (Magnus Gustaf) Mittag-Leffler
eyes.role: Swedish mathematician, member of the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, champion of Sofia Kovalevskaya
eyes.vantage_label: abroad: the man who passed the warning
eyes.authenticity: His letters to Pierre Curie and to Poincaré (8 and 12 September 1903 exchange) are documented by the Association Curie et Joliot-Curie from archival sources; his papers are at the Institut Mittag-Leffler. He was not a member of the Nobel physics committee.
eyes.bio: A long-time advocate for women in mathematics, he let Pierre know unofficially that a prize was in view and then sounded out Poincaré on how it should be shared. His letters are the documentary hinge of the 1903 credit question.

sources.title: Association Curie et Joliot-Curie — The 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics

eyes.name: André-Louis Debierne
eyes.role: Young chemist (aged 25 in 1899), Pierre Curie's former student, working on the Curies' pitchblende residues; later Marie's closest collaborator and successor at the Radium Institute
eyes.where: ESPCI and the Sorbonne laboratories, Paris
eyes.vantage_label: in the lab: the third discoverer in the residues
eyes.authenticity: Comptes rendus notes of 16 October 1899 and April 1900 (naming actinium). Later disputes over whether his 1899 substance was actinium or a mixture (Giesel's 1902 'emanium') are a known priority question.
eyes.bio: He found a third new radioactive substance in the same ore and named it actinium. After Pierre's death he stayed beside Marie in the laboratory; with her he isolated radium metal in 1910.

sources.title: ESPCI — History: ESPCI and the discovery of chemical elements

eyes.name: Irène Curie (later Joliot-Curie)
eyes.role: The Curies' elder daughter: an infant in the notebook years, aged 8 when her father died, 17 when she went to the front in 1914
eyes.where: Boulevard Kellermann, Paris; later the war zone
eyes.vantage_label: child in the household, later a witness and successor
eyes.form: recorded in her mother's notebooks; later letters
eyes.authenticity: Marie kept a notebook of Irène's growth with the care of a lab record (AIP). Irène's own later writings and letters are twentieth-century publications and are digested only.
eyes.bio: Her infancy is logged in the same hand as the radium measurements. She became her mother's radiographer in 1914 and in 1934, with Frédéric Joliot, discovered artificial radioactivity — the bridge from this chapter to fission.

sources.title: AIP exhibit — A Student in Paris (1891–1897)
AIP exhibit — War Duty (1914–1919)

eyes.name: Comptes rendus hebdomadaires des séances de l'Académie des sciences
eyes.role: The Académie's weekly record: notes by non-members had to be presented by a member, and the sitting date fixed priority
eyes.where: Institut de France, quai de Conti, Paris
eyes.vantage_label: institutional eye: the dated ledger of the race
eyes.authenticity: Printed proceedings, freely digitised. Here used for sitting dates and who presented what.
eyes.bio: An institution, not a person: every Monday it stamped a date on who claimed what. Marie Curie could not present her own work; Lippmann and Becquerel did it for her, and that mechanism is itself part of the story.

sources.title: Comptes rendus Physique — historical article on Becquerel's discovery

entries.headline: A screen glows across a darkened room
entries.digest: Working alone in the evening with a discharge tube shrouded in black card, Röntgen noticed a fluorescent screen lighting up some distance away. Nothing visible could have reached it. He spent the following weeks testing what the new rays would pass through — paper, wood, flesh — and what stopped them, telling almost no one. Because he later had his personal papers burned, the evening survives through his paper and his institute's records rather than a notebook.
entries.source_note: Würzburg exhibition catalogue (date and setting); https://www.uni-wuerzburg.de/fileadmin/uniwue/Presse/pdf-Dateien/Roentgen-Ausstellungskatalog_en.pdf

entries.headline: His wife's hand, bones and wedding ring
entries.digest: Röntgen made an exposure of his wife Anna Bertha's hand: the bones show pale, and the ring floats around one finger. It became the image that carried the discovery around the world within weeks. It is also the first sign that this decade's discoveries would be read in human bodies.
entries.source_note: Würzburg catalogue; https://www.uni-wuerzburg.de/fileadmin/uniwue/Presse/pdf-Dateien/Roentgen-Ausstellungskatalog_en.pdf

entries.headline: Manuscript handed to the local society
entries.digest: Röntgen submitted 'Über eine neue Art von Strahlen (vorläufige Mitteilung)' to the Würzburg Physical-Medical Society, which printed it at once. By choosing a provincial society's proceedings he secured priority in days rather than months. He called the unknown radiation 'X'.
entries.source_note: Würzburg catalogue; https://www.uni-wuerzburg.de/fileadmin/uniwue/Presse/pdf-Dateien/Roentgen-Ausstellungskatalog_en.pdf

entries.headline: A hundred envelopes, with photographs enclosed
entries.digest: On New Year's Day he posted about a hundred offprints to colleagues, tucking in prints of the hand and other radiographs; his outgoing mail book of these years survives. Within the month the pictures were in the newspapers and on the table of the Paris Académie. It is the moment a private result became a public race.
entries.source_note: Würzburg catalogue (mail book 1888–1900 in University Archives); https://www.uni-wuerzburg.de/fileadmin/uniwue/Presse/pdf-Dateien/Roentgen-Ausstellungskatalog_en.pdf

entries.headline: Poincaré shows the X-ray pictures; a question is asked
entries.digest: At the Académie, Henri Poincaré displayed X-ray photographs and raised the idea that the rays might be linked to the fluorescence of the glass where they emerged. Becquerel, whose family had studied phosphorescence for three generations, took the hint: perhaps phosphorescent substances gave off penetrating rays too. He chose uranium salts, which he knew well.
entries.source_note: laradioactivite.com timeline; APS News (Becquerel heard of X-rays at an Académie meeting in January); https://laradioactivite-prod-en.apps.wok3.in2p3.fr/articles/phenomenon/uranic_rays

entries.headline: The only public lecture; Kölliker's hand
entries.digest: Röntgen gave the one public lecture he ever devoted to the discovery. During it he radiographed the hand of the elderly anatomist Albert von Kölliker, who proposed that the rays bear Röntgen's name. Röntgen himself kept calling them X-rays.
entries.source_note: Würzburg catalogue; https://www.uni-wuerzburg.de/fileadmin/uniwue/Presse/pdf-Dateien/Roentgen-Ausstellungskatalog_en.pdf

entries.headline: Sunlit uranium salts darken a wrapped plate
entries.digest: Becquerel reported that crystals of a uranium salt, set on a photographic plate wrapped in thick black paper and left in the sun, produced a silhouette on development. He read this as phosphorescence excited by sunlight emitting something like Röntgen's rays. The interpretation was wrong; the observation was right.
entries.source_note: Comptes rendus 122, 420–421; Giunta annotations; https://web.lemoyne.edu/GIUNTA/EA/BECQUERELann.HTML

entries.headline: Grey skies: the experiment goes into a drawer
entries.digest: He prepared new plates with uranium crusts, one with a thin copper cross between salt and plate, but the sun showed only fitfully. He put the whole arrangement away in a dark drawer and left the crusts in place. The sun stayed hidden for the next few days.
entries.source_note: Becquerel's own account in the note of 2 March 1896; Giunta; https://web.lemoyne.edu/GIUNTA/EA/BECQUERELann.HTML

entries.headline: Expecting nothing, he finds intense silhouettes
entries.digest: Becquerel developed the drawer plates, expecting at most faint images. Instead the silhouettes were strong — the copper cross stood out clearly. The uranium had been radiating in the dark, with no sunlight to excite it. He had a sitting to report to the next day.
entries.source_note: Giunta annotations; APS News; https://www.aps.org/publications/apsnews/200803/physicshistory.cfm

entries.headline: Rays without sunlight read into the record
entries.digest: Becquerel's second note was read: uranium salts kept in darkness still act through black paper on a photographic plate. The Académie's weekly date stamped it, and over the spring he followed with further notes. The discovery drew far less public excitement than X-rays, which is partly why it was still open ground eighteen months later.
entries.source_note: Comptes rendus 122 (1896), note of 2 March; Giunta; https://web.lemoyne.edu/GIUNTA/EA/BECQUERELann.HTML

entries.headline: Uranium itself is the source
entries.digest: By late spring Becquerel announced that the effect belonged to the element uranium rather than to phosphorescence, since non-phosphorescent uranium compounds and the metal itself showed it. He then largely moved on. The phenomenon became known as 'Becquerel rays' or 'uranium rays'.
entries.source_note: APS News (May 1896; element uranium); exact sitting date 18 May from standard histories, not directly checked; https://www.aps.org/publications/apsnews/200803/physicshistory.cfm

entries.headline: A baby enters the household ledger
entries.digest: Irène Curie was born in September 1897, months before her mother began her thesis research. Marie followed every stage of the infant's growth in a notebook with the same care she gave her experiments. The household's records and the laboratory's would soon run in the same hand.
entries.source_note: AIP, 'A Student in Paris' (September 1897; developmental notebook); day 12 Sept from standard biographies; https://history.aip.org/exhibits/curie/stud2_text.htm

entries.date_display: December 1897 (first notebook entries commonly dated 16 December)
entries.headline: The thesis begins with an electrometer
entries.digest: In a damp ground-floor storeroom at the ESPCI, Marie set up an ionisation chamber and Pierre's quartz electrometer to measure how strongly uranium rays make air conduct. Her research began about the end of 1897, and the joint notebooks — now at the BnF — date from these months. Measuring current, not blackening plates, was the decision that made everything quantitative.
entries.source_note: AIP ('about the end of 1897'); BnF (notebooks 1897–1898); 16 December is the date usually given for the first entry but was not confirmed in an accessible source; https://www.bnf.fr/fr/un-heritage-qui-rayonne-les-carnets-de-marie-curie

entries.headline: Pitchblende is more active than uranium
entries.digest: Marie began systematically testing minerals and compounds. The ore pitchblende proved far more active than pure uranium — an anomaly she would not explain away. It suggested an unknown, stronger substance hiding in the ore.
entries.source_note: Adloff, Chemistry International 2011 (11 February start of systematic testing); https://brianhill.github.io/manhattan-project/resources/PoloniumAndRadium.pdf

entries.headline: Thorium emits Becquerel rays — the German claim
entries.digest: Schmidt told the German Physical Society that thorium compounds emit rays like uranium's. Until then only uranium-bearing substances were known to do so. He was nineteen days ahead of Paris.
entries.source_note: GDCh Mitteilungen 25 (2017); Giunta note 26 (24 March vs 12 April); https://archiv.gdch.de/fileadmin/downloads/Netzwerk_und_Strukturen/Fachgruppen/Geschichte_der_Chemie/Mitteilungen_Band_25/2017-25-10.pdf

entries.place: Académie des sciences, Paris (presented by Lippmann)
entries.headline: Her first note: thorium, and an ore that is too strong
entries.digest: Gabriel Lippmann presented Marie's note on rays from uranium and thorium compounds; as a non-member, and a woman, she could not present it herself. She too had found thorium active — independently, but after Schmidt. The note's lasting point was the other one: pitchblende and chalcolite are much more active than uranium, so they must contain something new.
entries.source_note: Comptes rendus 126, 1101–1103; Giunta translation and notes; https://web.lemoyne.edu/GIUNTA/EA/CURIEann.HTML

entries.headline: The chemistry of pitchblende begins
entries.digest: Pierre, Marie and Gustave Bémont began separating pitchblende chemically, testing each fraction with the electrometer to follow the activity. Bémont, ESPCI's head of practical chemistry, brought the analytical method neither Curie had trained in. The notebooks from here on track activity through precipitates and filtrates.
entries.source_note: Adloff 2011 (trio began pitchblende chemistry 14 April); ESPCI history; https://brianhill.github.io/manhattan-project/resources/PoloniumAndRadium.pdf

entries.headline: Schmidt's paper appears in print
entries.digest: Schmidt's full paper on thorium radiation came out in the Annalen der Physik und Chemie. In print, it followed Marie's Paris note; at the lectern, it had preceded it. The GDCh history credits Schmidt with the thorium discovery, shortly before Curie, and Curie with the step into pitchblende.
entries.source_note: GDCh Mitteilungen 25 (2017); Annalen 65 (1898) 141–151; https://archiv.gdch.de/fileadmin/downloads/Netzwerk_und_Strukturen/Fachgruppen/Geschichte_der_Chemie/Mitteilungen_Band_25/2017-25-10.pdf

entries.headline: A run of experiments closes on a new element
entries.digest: Pierre had set aside his crystal work to join Marie. Between April and mid-July the notebooks track a substance that followed bismuth chemically but was hundreds of times more active than uranium. Demarçay's spectroscope showed no new lines, so the claim rested on radioactivity alone — a new kind of evidence for an element.
entries.source_note: Adloff 2011 (experiments 9 April–16 July; Demarçay found no new lines for polonium); https://brianhill.github.io/manhattan-project/resources/PoloniumAndRadium.pdf

entries.headline: 'Polonium', for an erased country — and a new word
entries.digest: The Curies' note 'Sur une substance nouvelle radio-active, contenue dans la pechblende' proposed the name polonium after Marie's Poland, then partitioned and absent from the map. The title carries the coinage 'radio-active', which they soon wrote without the hyphen. Pierre is first author; the measurements were hers.
entries.source_note: Adloff 2011 (title, 'radio-active' first appears here); https://brianhill.github.io/manhattan-project/resources/PoloniumAndRadium.pdf

entries.headline: Becquerel presents the polonium note
entries.digest: It was Becquerel, a member, who presented the Curies' polonium note to the Académie. The man whose rays had started the work now carried its first harvest into the record. The relationship would stay cordial in public and competitive underneath.
entries.source_note: ESPCI history (Becquerel presented the Curies' work, July 1898); https://www.espci.psl.eu/en/news/2019/history-espci-and-the-discovery-of-chemical

entries.headline: Two kinds of uranium ray: alpha and beta
entries.digest: Rutherford signed off a long paper on uranium radiation. By stacking thin foils over a uranium layer he showed the radiation is complex: one part is stopped almost at once, another penetrates much farther. He named them, provisionally, after the first two Greek letters. Within weeks he left for a professorship at McGill.
entries.quote: which will be termed for convenience the α radiation
entries.source_note: Phil. Mag. ser. 5, 47 (Jan 1899) 109–163, dated 'Cavendish Laboratory, September 1, 1898'; https://chemteam.info/Chem-History/Rutherford-Alpha&Beta.html

entries.headline: Radium: three names on the note
entries.digest: The note on a second, 'strongly radio-active' substance in pitchblende was signed by Pierre Curie, Marie Curie and Gustave Bémont. It concentrated with barium, and this time Eugène Demarçay found a spectral line belonging to no known element. They called it radium. Bémont's signature is the record's acknowledgement of the chemist at the bench.
entries.source_note: Adloff 2011 (26 December 1898; Demarçay's unassigned lines; Bémont's role); ESPCI (Bémont signed the note); https://www.espci.psl.eu/en/news/2019/history-espci-and-the-discovery-of-chemical

entries.headline: Boxing Day sitting stamps the radium claim
entries.digest: The Académie met the day after Christmas, and the radium note entered the Comptes rendus with that date. The new element existed as a line in a spectrum and a current in an electrometer; it would take Marie almost four years and tonnes of residue to produce a decigram of radium chloride and an atomic weight.
entries.source_note: ESPCI reference list (minutes of 26 December 1898); Adloff 2011; https://old.iupac.org/publications/ci/2011/3301/5_adloff.html

entries.headline: A radiation that halves in about a minute
entries.digest: Now at McGill, Rutherford signed off a paper on an 'emanation' given off by thorium compounds — a radioactive gas. Its activity fell away regularly: half gone in about a minute, half the rest in the next. This is the first clear measurement of what would later be called a half-life, a constant fixed for each substance.
entries.quote: fallen to one-half its value after an interval of about one minute
entries.source_note: Phil. Mag. ser. 5, 49 (Jan 1900) 1–14, dated 'McGill University, Montreal, September 13, 1899'; https://web.chemteam.info/Chem-History/Rutherford-half-life.html

entries.headline: A third new substance in the residues
entries.digest: Debierne, working through the same pitchblende residues the Curies had obtained, reported a new radioactive substance that went with the iron-group and rare-earth fractions. The Curies' workshop was becoming a small school. Whether this first material was the same as what was later called actinium was debated afterwards.
entries.source_note: ESPCI history (Académie reference of 16 October 1899); https://www.espci.psl.eu/en/news/2019/history-espci-and-the-discovery-of-chemical

entries.headline: He names it actinium
entries.digest: In a further note Debierne proposed the name actinium, from the Greek for 'ray'. In Germany Friedrich Giesel later isolated a substance he called emanium, and the priority between them became one of the era's minor quarrels. The book records both positions.
entries.source_note: ESPCI history (April 1900 name proposed); exact sitting not checked; https://www.espci.psl.eu/en/news/2019/history-espci-and-the-discovery-of-chemical

entries.headline: A young Oxford chemist takes a post in Montreal
entries.digest: After a trip to Canada in spring 1900, Soddy took a demonstrator's post at McGill. He soon began working with Rutherford on the puzzle of thorium's activity. Rutherford needed a chemist; Soddy needed a problem.
entries.source_note: Chemistry World, 'Transmutations and isotopes'; https://www.chemistryworld.com/feature/transmutations-and-isotopes/3004868.article

entries.headline: Thorium X: a different element is appearing
entries.digest: Soddy and Rutherford separated from thorium a strongly active material, thorium X, and watched the thorium regain activity as the separated part lost it. Soddy later recalled exclaiming that this was transmutation, and Rutherford warning him not to use a word that smelled of alchemy. That exchange survives only as Soddy's late recollection.
entries.source_note: Chemistry World (exchange recalled 'years later'); dates approximate; https://www.chemistryworld.com/feature/transmutations-and-isotopes/3004868.article

entries.headline: Atoms are changing into other atoms
entries.digest: Rutherford and Soddy published 'The Cause and Nature of Radioactivity'. They argued that radioactivity is a property of the atom and that it goes with chemical change: new kinds of matter are produced continuously, and the change happens inside the atom. It was the end of the indivisible, permanent atom.
entries.quote: Radioactivity may therefore be considered as a manifestation of subatomic chemical change
entries.source_note: Phil. Mag. 4 (1902) 370–396; Giunta excerpt; month approximate; https://web.lemoyne.edu/GIUNTA/ruthsod.html

entries.headline: Sore fingers, a spilled demonstration
entries.digest: Pierre lectured on radium at the Royal Institution in London. His health was bad: he struggled to dress, and his fingers were covered in sores from handling radium. During the demonstration some radium was spilled. Later he often lay awake in pain.
entries.source_note: AIP, 'Recognition and Disappointment' (June 1903 RI talk; sores; spill); exact day not given; https://history.aip.org/exhibits/curie/recdis1_text.htm

entries.headline: Doctor of physical science, in a black dress
entries.digest: Marie defended her thesis, 'Recherches sur les substances radioactives', the first doctorate in physical science earned by a woman in France. Her sister Bronya had come from Poland and wanted her in a new dress; Marie chose a black one she could wear in the laboratory afterwards. The thesis gathered five years of notebook work into one argument.
entries.source_note: AIP, 'Recognition and Disappointment' (June 1903, Bronya, black dress); date 25 June per task brief and standard histories; https://history.aip.org/exhibits/curie/recdis1_text.htm

entries.headline: A guest at the celebration dinner
entries.digest: Rutherford, visiting Paris, was a last-minute guest at the dinner marking Marie's doctorate. He had seen the ESPCI shed and asked how they had managed to work in it. The later-told story — Pierre in the garden at nightfall holding up a tube of radium that glowed, his hands scarred — comes from Rutherford's recollections and Ève Curie's 1937 book, not from a dated note.
entries.source_note: AIP (last-minute guest; remark on lacking a laboratory); glowing-tube scene from later biographies (flagged); https://history.aip.org/exhibits/curie/recdis1_text.htm

entries.headline: 'Consider us together'
entries.digest: Pierre answered a letter from Mittag-Leffler, who had told him privately that he was under consideration for the Nobel Prize. He asked that he be considered jointly with Marie for their work on radioactive bodies, pointing to her part in discovering the new elements. He added that separating them would surprise many people, and that he himself expected nothing.
entries.source_note: Association Curie et Joliot-Curie, 'The 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics'; https://curie-joliotcurie.fr/?p=1179

entries.headline: Sounding out Poincaré on how to split it
entries.digest: Mittag-Leffler wrote to Henri Poincaré asking whether it would be fairer to give the prize to the two Curies alone or to divide it with Becquerel. Poincaré replied on 12 September that a division with Becquerel was fairer. Mittag-Leffler was not on the Nobel committee; his influence was by letter and connection.
entries.source_note: Association Curie et Joliot-Curie; https://curie-joliotcurie.fr/?p=1179

entries.headline: Yes — but not to Stockholm in December
entries.digest: The Swedish Academy had voted on 12 November to award the physics prize to Becquerel and both Curies; its secretary Aurivillius wrote on the 14th. Pierre replied on the 19th asking to postpone the ceremony and lecture: teaching and ill health kept them in Paris. The Nobel archive also lists a 1903 nomination by Charles Bouchard naming all three.
entries.source_note: Association Curie et Joliot-Curie (12, 14, 19 Nov); Nobel nomination archive id 2993; https://nobelprize.org/nomination/archive/show.php?id=2993

entries.headline: Becquerel collects his half; the Curies are absent
entries.digest: At the ceremony in Stockholm, Becquerel received his share in person. The French minister, Marchand, accepted on behalf of the absent Curies. Half the prize went to Becquerel, half jointly to Pierre and Marie.
entries.source_note: Association Curie et Joliot-Curie; https://curie-joliotcurie.fr/?p=1179

entries.headline: The delayed Nobel lecture: a warning in it
entries.digest: Pierre finally gave the required lecture in Stockholm. He ended by asking whether humanity benefits from knowing nature's secrets, noting that radium could be dangerous in criminal hands, and concluded that he believed discoveries would bring more good than harm. Marie and he travelled together; Ève had been born the previous December.
entries.source_note: Nobel Foundation lecture (French original), not fetched here; Pierre proposed Easter or mid-June (Association Curie et Joliot-Curie); https://curie-joliotcurie.fr/?p=1179

entries.headline: Rain, an umbrella, a six-ton wagon
entries.digest: After a luncheon, Pierre went to his publisher and found the doors shut by a strike. Crossing the street in heavy rain behind his umbrella, he stepped into the path of a horse-drawn wagon loaded with military uniforms. He was killed instantly. He was forty-six.
entries.source_note: AIP, 'Tragedy and Adjustment' (date, rain, wagon c. six tons, strike); street from standard histories; https://history.aip.org/exhibits/curie/trag1_text.htm

entries.headline: The news at home
entries.digest: Marie learned that evening. In shock she sent Irène to neighbours, telegraphed her family in Poland and had Pierre's body brought home. She broke down only when his brother Jacques arrived from Montpellier the next day. She went back to the laboratory the day after the funeral.
entries.source_note: AIP, 'Tragedy and Adjustment'; https://history.aip.org/exhibits/curie/trag1_text.htm

entries.headline: A child sent to the neighbours
entries.digest: Irène, eight, was taken to stay with neighbours while her mother received the body. The family accounts say she was told gradually. Her father's death would shape the laboratory life she grew up inside.
entries.source_note: AIP (Irène sent to neighbours); later family accounts; https://history.aip.org/exhibits/curie/trag1_text.htm

entries.date_display: Late April 1906 onward (commonly dated from 30 April)
entries.headline: A journal addressed to Pierre
entries.digest: Within days Marie began a private journal written to Pierre in the second person. Its eight entries record spring flowers he would have liked, visits to his grave, the pain of sunny days, the comfort of the laboratory, and her appointment to his chair. It is a twentieth-century publication, so it is digested here and not quoted.
entries.source_note: Diaries of Note (eight entries; BnF; extracts in Ève Curie 1937); start date approximate; https://diariesofnote.com/2023/05/14/i-no-longer-love-the-sun-or-the-flowers/

entries.headline: The Sorbonne offers her Pierre's post
entries.digest: The Faculty of Science invited Marie to take over Pierre's teaching — the first time a woman would teach there. She had already refused a state pension, saying she could support herself and her children. Her journal records the appointment as something she would have wanted to tell him.
entries.source_note: AIP, 'Tragedy and Adjustment' (13 May 1906 invitation; pension refused); https://history.aip.org/exhibits/curie/trag1_text.htm

entries.headline: The first lecture begins where his stopped
entries.digest: Marie gave her first lecture in Pierre's course to a packed hall that included the curious and the press. By the standard account she began at the point where his last lecture had ended, without any opening tribute. It is the public counterpart to the private journal.
entries.source_note: Standard biographies (date and 'resumed where he left off'); not confirmed in a fetched source

entries.headline: Radium metal, with Marie
entries.digest: Debierne and Marie isolated radium as a metal, settling doubts from rivals that radium was truly an element rather than a compound. He had stayed at her side through the years after Pierre's death. The work fed directly into her second prize.
entries.source_note: ESPCI history and standard histories; exact date not checked; https://www.espci.psl.eu/en/news/2019/history-espci-and-the-discovery-of-chemical

entries.headline: Coda: a second Nobel Prize, in chemistry
entries.digest: Marie received the 1911 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for the discovery of polonium and radium and the isolation of radium. This time she went to Stockholm and lectured herself, giving credit for shared work by name. She remains the only person with Nobel Prizes in two different sciences.
entries.source_note: Standard Nobel record; date not fetched here

entries.headline: Coda: Röntgen's rays go to war
entries.digest: Irène, seventeen, became her mother's first radiological assistant. In autumn 1914 they made their first trip to the front with a military doctor, using X-ray cars that soldiers called 'petites Curies'; the first was ready by late October. Neither was adequately shielded.
entries.source_note: AIP, 'War Duty (1914–1919)'; https://history.aip.org/exhibits/curie/war1_text.htm

claims.evidence: Sitzungsberichte der Würzburger Physikalisch-Medizinischen Gesellschaft; Würzburg catalogue

claims.claim: Sunlit uranium salts emit radiation that passes black paper (read as phosphorescence)
Uranium salts emit the radiation in darkness, without sunlight
claims.evidence: Comptes rendus 122 (note of 2 March 1896); plates developed 1 March

claims.claim: Electrometer measurements of uranium rays begin in the joint notebooks
claims.evidence: BnF Curie notebooks (dated 1897–1898); 16 December is the commonly cited first entry
Deutsche Physikalische Gesellschaft; Annalen der Physik 65 (1898) 141–151, 23 April 1898

claims.claim: Thorium is active (independently, after Schmidt); pitchblende and chalcolite more active than uranium
Polonium, a new element; first use of the term 'radio-active'
claims.evidence: Comptes rendus 127, P. Curie and Mme S. Curie, presented by Becquerel

claims.claim: Uranium radiation consists of at least two types, named alpha and beta
claims.evidence: Phil. Mag. ser. 5, 47 (1899) 109–163, dated Cavendish Laboratory

claims.claim: Radium, a second new element, confirmed by a new spectral line (Demarçay)
claims.evidence: Comptes rendus 127, P. Curie, Mme P. Curie, G. Bémont

claims.claim: Thorium emanation's activity halves in about one minute — the half-life concept
claims.evidence: Phil. Mag. ser. 5, 49 (1900) 1–14, dated McGill University

claims.claim: A new radioactive substance in pitchblende residues (named actinium, April 1900)
claims.evidence: Comptes rendus 129 (1899); priority later contested with Giesel's 'emanium'

claims.claim: Radioactivity is subatomic chemical change — atoms transmute (with Soddy)
Helium is produced by radioactive decay (with Ramsay, London)
Asks that Marie be considered jointly with him for the Nobel Prize
claims.evidence: Pierre Curie to Mittag-Leffler, documented by Association Curie et Joliot-Curie; Bouchard nomination of all three in Nobel archive

convergences.label: The drawer plates and the Académie sitting
convergences.note: One day separates the private surprise (Sunday development) from the public claim (Monday sitting): the weekly rhythm of the Académie set the pace of discovery.

convergences.label: The thorium race, spring 1898
convergences.note: Schmidt spoke on 24 March, Curie's note was presented on 12 April, and Schmidt's paper was printed on 23 April. Each can be called first by a different measure; what Curie added was the pitchblende anomaly.

convergences.label: Polonium and the word 'radio-active'
convergences.note: The notebook run closed on 16 July and was read into the record two days later — by Becquerel, whose rays had started it.

convergences.label: Autumn 1898: Paris names elements, Cambridge names rays
convergences.note: Within weeks of each other, the Curies were naming a new element and Rutherford was dividing the radiation into alpha and beta. Neither yet knew what the rays were.

convergences.label: Radium
convergences.note: Three signatures on one note: the institutional record names the assistant chemist that later legend often drops.

convergences.label: Autumn 1899: Montreal and Paris
convergences.note: Rutherford measures a half-period in Montreal while Debierne pulls a third new substance from the same residues in Paris; the field had become two schools.

convergences.label: Thesis day and the dinner
convergences.note: The French doctorate, the British-Canadian rival at the table, and Pierre's scarred hands: the most famous evening in the story is also the least documented, resting on later recollections.

convergences.label: The Nobel letters, August–December 1903
convergences.note: Pierre's letter, Mittag-Leffler's exchange with Poincaré, and Becquerel alone in Stockholm: three documents that together decided how credit was shared.

convergences.label: Rue Dauphine
convergences.note: A street accident on a rainy Thursday, and the household that absorbed it: Marie's grief went into a private journal and a public lecture hall.

ties.note: Married 1895; co-authors and joint keepers of the laboratory notebooks.
Mother and daughter; Irène's growth was logged in Marie's notebook, and she later became her radiographer and successor.
Marie chose Becquerel's rays as her thesis subject; he presented the polonium note and shared the 1903 prize.
Röntgen's photographs, shown by Poincaré on 20 January 1896, prompted Becquerel's search.
Independent rivals on thorium in spring 1898, separated by nineteen days.
Co-signatory of the radium note; ran the chemistry with the Curies at ESPCI.
Worked on the Curies' residues; after 1906 her closest collaborator.
Rival and admirer; guest at the dinner of 25 June 1903.
Corresponded in summer 1903 about the Nobel Prize.
Rutherford's first research at the Cavendish used X-rays to ionise gases, the method he carried over to uranium rays.

threads_out.note: Irène Curie and Frédéric Joliot's artificial radioactivity (1934) and Rutherford's alpha-particle programme led directly to neutron bombardment of uranium; the half-life and transmutation ideas of 1899–1902 are the grammar of the fission papers.
Marie and seventeen-year-old Irène took mobile X-ray cars, the 'petites Curies', to the front from autumn 1914 — Röntgen's rays of 1895 turned to battlefield surgery.
Röntgen's rays became, via X-ray diffraction (von Laue and the Braggs, 1912–13), the tool Rosalind Franklin and Raymond Gosling used to photograph DNA.
